# Move from Promptfoo or Marsfoo

> Import saved Evals results, convert a config to native suite files, and review which verdicts can be compared.

Source: [Web version](https://docs.martiansecurity.ai/migrate/promptfoo/)

Python SDK · Any developer with promptfoo results or config files; no Martian account or API key; a model key only for a converted llm-rubric judge

Two commands move a promptfoo project. `martian evals import promptfoo` brings the results you already have into the local Evals UI, one run per provider. `martian evals convert promptfoo` turns your config’s tests into [suite files](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/sdk/local-evals.md) that `martian evals run` runs against your agent, wherever its assertions have an equivalent check, and lists everything it leaves out.

Neither command runs promptfoo or calls its providers, and promptfoo does not need to be installed next to the SDK.

For a promptfoo **red team** config or its results, see [Move a promptfoo red team](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/migrate/promptfoo-redteam.md).

Needs SDK 0.1.4 or later

The original walkthrough uses **martian-sdk 0.1.4**. For archive deduplication, additional provider and assertion support, and Compare, see [Migrate with the current SDK](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/migrate/promptfoo.md#migrate-with-the-current-sdk).

## Migrate with the current SDK

These steps use SDK 0.4.0 or later and its [bundled workbench](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/local-sdk.md#open-the-bundled-workbench). The import and conversion commands accept supported Marsfoo exports and configs under the same `promptfoo` subcommand.

### 1\. Import archived results

Use a version 3 results JSON archive. To include attachments, use an export made with `promptfoo export eval EVAL_ID --include-media -o results.json`. Keep the archive, local data folder and generated suites private because they can contain prompts, replies or attachments.

```sh
martian evals import promptfoo results.json --data-dir ./evals-data
```

Each provider becomes a saved run with its original case verdicts. Reimporting unchanged evidence reuses the runs and reviews. Changed evidence makes a separate snapshot. Use `--new-id` to create independent copies, including when you need comparison evidence produced by the newer importer.

Start the [bundled workbench](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/local-sdk.md#open-the-bundled-workbench) with `./evals-data`. Select **Evals → Runs**, open a run and select **Inspect** on a case. **View trace** opens the archived span tree when the export linked one. **Imported media** shows the case’s attachments, including unavailable references when the export omitted the bytes. **Overview** shows named and derived metrics when the archive includes them.

### 2\. Preview config conversion and grade the suite

```sh
martian evals convert promptfoo promptfooconfig.yaml --provider echo --strict --dry-run --output suite
```

Replace `echo` with the source provider’s exact ID or label. A plain `echo` provider uses the rendered prompt as the stored reply, with `providerOutput` taking precedence. Supported JSON POST and OpenAI-compatible chat configurations create native HTTP targets. You can use `--target agent.py:answer` for a trusted local Python adapter. Use `--all-providers` instead of selecting one provider or adapter to convert each supported provider into separate suites.

**Strict mode** exits with code **2** on unsupported settings or known scoring differences. **Dry run** lists the planned suites and writes no files. Review any listed omissions, remove `--dry-run` when ready, and run the suite paths printed by conversion. The single-provider example uses the same store as the imported results.

```sh
martian evals run suite/evals.yaml --data-dir ./evals-data
```

Conversion maps supported text and structured assertions, including literal JSON Schema, embedded JSON, [XML](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/sdk/local-evals-yaml.md#check-structured-replies), word count and edit distance. It preserves supported provider and prompt selectors, assertion weights, test thresholds, one level of assertion sets, named metrics, and arithmetic derived metrics. The SDK reports custom code, unsupported schema rules and constraints, and configurations that need verdict review. If an unsupported assertion contributes to a weighted gate, best-effort conversion skips that test and strict conversion refuses it.

### 3\. Compare saved verdicts

In **Evals → Compare**, select the imported run as **Baseline**, the native run as **Candidate**, and choose **Compare runs**. For runs with different dataset identities, the workbench verifies the shared cases’ rendered prompts, variables, effective deterministic checks, weights and thresholds before pairing verdicts. The **Case verdict** view labels verified comparisons and shows which cases were present on only one side.

An archived grade stays as recorded. In a comparison with verified check rules, a missing case verdict is incomparable. If any shared case lacks verified grading evidence or uses different rules, the entire cross-dataset comparison is unavailable. For example, a saved XML grade that disagrees with the native parser, or an embedded JSON schema referenced only by a file path, lacks the evidence required for that comparison. Model graders and custom transforms can also block verification.

The sections below show the original 0.1.4 walkthrough and its conversion limits.

## Before you start

-   Use **Python 3.12 or newer** and Bash or Zsh on macOS or Linux.
-   To import results, you need the JSON file that `promptfoo eval -o results.json` writes. Other output formats, and results files from promptfoo releases that wrote the older results table, are refused.
-   To convert a config, you need your `promptfooconfig.yaml` and a Python function that calls your agent.
-   You need no Martian account or API key. A converted suite needs a model key only if it keeps an `llm-rubric` assertion as an LLM judge; that judge sends each case to the model provider you choose.
-   The data folder (default `~/.martian/evals`) and the converted suite’s results hold prompts and replies in clear text. Keep them private.

## 1\. Install the SDK

In your promptfoo project’s folder, create an isolated environment and install the SDK:

```sh
python3 --version
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install --upgrade 'martian-sdk[evals]'
martian --version
```

Check for Python 3.12 or newer and SDK **0.1.4** or later. Keep this environment active for the remaining commands.

The examples on this page use this config. It has one prompt, two versions of a bot as providers, and three tests:

```yaml
description: FAQ bot

prompts:
  - "Answer the customer briefly. Question: {{question}}"

providers:
  - id: file://provider.py:bot_v1
    label: bot-v1
  - id: file://provider.py:bot_v2
    label: bot-v2

defaultTest:
  assert:
    - type: not-icontains
      value: as an AI
    - type: latency
      threshold: 2000

tests:
  - description: opening hours
    vars:
      question: When do you open?
    assert:
      - type: icontains
        value: 9am
  - description: delivery
    vars:
      question: Do you deliver?
    assert:
      - type: regex
        value: "\\d+ km"
      - type: javascript
        value: output.length < 100
  - description: card payments
    vars:
      question: Can I pay by card?
    assert:
      - type: icontains
        value: card
      - type: levenshtein
        value: Yes, we take all major cards.
        threshold: 5
```

## 2\. Import your results

```sh
martian evals import promptfoo results.json
```

The first time, log lines from the local evaluation store appear while it creates the data folder. Then each provider in the file prints one line:

```text
results.json: provider bot-v1, run promptfoo-bot-v1-1, 3 cases: 2 passed, 1 failed, 0 errors
results.json: provider bot-v2, run promptfoo-bot-v2-1, 3 cases: 3 passed, 0 failed, 0 errors
Open them in the local Evals UI: martian ui
```

The exit code is **`0`**. Each run is named `promptfoo-`, the provider’s label (or its ID when it has none) and a number that counts that provider’s imported runs. In SDK 0.4.0 and later, providers with the same label get additional provider numbers. If provider IDs also repeat, the archive must include enough prompt-column information to distinguish them.

-   One command can take several results files. Every file is read before anything is written: if one cannot be imported, the command exits **`2`**, says which file and why, and imports none of them.
-   In SDK 0.4.0 and later, reimporting unchanged results reuses the completed runs and preserves their traces and reviews. Changes to archived results create a separate snapshot. Use `--new-id` to import independent copies.
-   To import into a folder other than `~/.martian/evals`, add `--data-dir DIR`, or set `MARTIAN_EVALS_HOME`. Open the UI with the same folder.

## 3\. Open the runs

```sh
martian ui
```

Your browser opens `http://127.0.0.1:7600/`. The UI has one user and no login; stop it with Ctrl+C in the terminal.

1.  **Runs** lists one run for each provider in the **Default** project. The config’s `description` appears under each run’s name.
2.  Select a run. Each case’s input is the prompt with its vars filled in. The prompt text is the same under every provider, so the same test has the same case ID in every run of the file. The expected column shows the test’s assertions, and the verdict is promptfoo’s own verdict on that row.
3.  Select a row’s **Inspect** button, which opens the case. Each assertion promptfoo graded is an assessment that passed or failed, with promptfoo’s reason.
4.  Open **Compare**, choose the runs of two providers as **Baseline** and **Candidate**, and select **Compare runs**. Providers that ran the same tests on the same prompts pair case by case, whether they come from one results file or from two. A case on which a provider errored counts as **Not Comparable**.

## 4\. Convert your config

Write a Python file that calls your agent. The converted suite calls the function once per case with two keyword arguments, `prompt` (the prompt with the test’s vars filled in) and `vars` (the test’s vars), and grades the text it returns. This `agent.py` answers from a table; replace the body with a call to your application:

```python
REPLIES = {
    "When do you open?": "We open at 9am.",
    "Do you deliver?": "Yes, within 5 km.",
    "Can I pay by card?": "Yes, we take all major cards.",
}


def answer(prompt, vars):
    return REPLIES.get(vars["question"], "I don't know.")
```

Convert the config into a new folder:

```sh
martian evals convert promptfoo promptfooconfig.yaml --target agent.py:answer --output suite
```

The command prints the suite files it wrote and everything it did not convert:

```text
suite/evals.yaml: promptfoo tests 1, 3, 2 cases in cases.jsonl, checks not_icontains, latency, icontains
suite/evals-2.yaml: promptfoo tests 2, 1 cases in cases-2.jsonl, checks not_icontains, latency, regex
Not converted (also listed at the top of each suite file):
- providers[0] bot-v1 (file://provider.py:bot_v1): not called: the suite calls agent.py:answer instead
- providers[1] bot-v2 (file://provider.py:bot_v2): not called: the suite calls agent.py:answer instead
- tests[1].assert[1] javascript: runs custom code, which a suite file's built-in checks do not; write the rule as a custom Python scorer, `def scorer(inputs, outputs, expectations)` (name only the arguments it reads; `trace` too) returning True or False, a number, or a pair of either with a reason, and add it with `type: python` (`file:` and `function:`) by hand; this converter does not translate the code
- tests[2].assert[1] levenshtein: scores closeness to a reference text, or perplexity; no built-in check does
Run each with `martian evals run`, such as: martian evals run suite/evals.yaml
```

A suite file applies every check to every case, while promptfoo sets assertions per test. The converter therefore groups tests that need the same kinds of checks into one suite: `evals.yaml` with `cases.jsonl`, then `evals-2.yaml` with `cases-2.jsonl`, and so on. A check whose value differs between the tests of one suite, such as `icontains` above, reads the value from each case. The `defaultTest` assertions come first in every suite.

| Option | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--target FILE.py[:FUNCTION]` | The function each case calls, as above. Without a function name, it calls `target`. Without `--target`, a test’s `providerOutput` is graded as a stored reply, and a test without one is not converted |
| `--judge-model MODEL` | The model for `llm-rubric` assertions, such as `openai:/YOUR_JUDGE_MODEL`. Without it, `llm-rubric` is not converted |
| `--output DIR` | The folder for the suite and case files. A folder that already holds one of those files is refused, and nothing is written |

## 5\. Run the converted suites

Run each suite file:

```sh
martian evals run suite/evals.yaml
martian evals run suite/evals-2.yaml
```

The first suite prints this table and exits **`0`**:

```text
                       evals.yaml: 2 cases
┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
┃ Check         ┃ Passed ┃ Failed ┃ Errors ┃ Pass rate (95% CI) ┃
┡━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┩
│ not_icontains │ 2      │ 0      │ 0      │ 100% (34–100%)     │
│ latency       │ 2      │ 0      │ 0      │ 100% (34–100%)     │
│ icontains     │ 2      │ 0      │ 0      │ 100% (34–100%)     │
│ All checks    │ 2      │ 0      │ 0      │ 100% (34–100%)     │
└───────────────┴────────┴────────┴────────┴────────────────────┘
```

Each suite writes its result files next to it (`suite/results`, `suite/results-2`) and records a run in the local Evals UI. [Run evals locally with a suite file](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/sdk/local-evals.md) explains the results, exit codes and options.

## 6\. Replace what did not convert

Each item in the list needs a decision: rewrite it as a check, or leave it out. Custom code, such as the `javascript` assertion above, becomes a Python check. Write the rule as a function that takes the reply as `outputs` and returns `True` or `False`, in `suite/scorers.py`:

```python
def short_reply(outputs):
    return len(outputs) < 100
```

Add it at the end of the `checks` list in `suite/evals-2.yaml`, at the same indentation as the converted checks:

```yaml
- type: python
  name: short_reply
  file: scorers.py
  function: short_reply
```

The file path is relative to the suite file. Run the suite again:

```sh
martian evals run suite/evals-2.yaml
```

Because the checks changed, the earlier verdict is discarded and the case is graded again. The table gains a `short_reply` row with 1 passed. A Python check runs with your user’s full permissions, so review check files you did not write before you run them.

## What maps where

**Results.** Importing a results file maps it like this:

| In promptfoo results | In the local Evals UI |
| --- | --- |
| One provider | One run, named `promptfoo-<label>-<n>` |
| One test on one prompt | A case, `test <n>`. With several prompts, `test <n>, prompt <m>`, where the prompts are counted by their text and not by promptfoo’s numbering of each provider’s columns, so every provider’s run names the same test and prompt the same way; a later repeat adds `(repeat <k>)` |
| The rendered prompt and the vars | The case’s input |
| The test’s assertions | The case’s expected value |
| The provider’s output | The reply |
| promptfoo’s pass, fail or error for the row | The case’s verdict, so a test `threshold` counts as it did in promptfoo |
| Each graded assertion | An assessment named after its type, passed or failed, with promptfoo’s reason and numeric score. A second assertion of the same type is `<type> (2)`; one inside an `assert-set` is `assert-set/<type>` |
| A model-graded assertion or a red team grader | An LLM judge assessment |
| Latency, tokens and cost | The case’s trace |
| The config’s `description` | The run’s dataset name. The rest of the config is not copied |

**Assertions.** The converter turns an assertion into a check only when the check decides the same way:

| promptfoo assertion | Suite check |
| --- | --- |
| `contains`, `contains-all` | `contains`, case-sensitive |
| `icontains`, `icontains-all` | `contains` |
| `contains-any`, `icontains-any` | `contains` with `any_of: true`; case-sensitive for `contains-any` |
| `not-contains`, `not-contains-any` | `not_contains`, case-sensitive |
| `not-icontains`, `not-icontains-any` | `not_contains` |
| `regex`, `not-regex` | `matches`, `not_matches`, read as a Python regular expression |
| `equals`, `not-equals` with text, a number or a boolean | `matches`, `not_matches` on the whole reply |
| `starts-with`, `not-starts-with` | `matches`, `not_matches` at the start of the reply |
| `is-json` with no schema, or a schema of only `type: object` and `required` | `is_json`, with the required keys |
| `llm-rubric` with a text rubric | The `rubric` judge on `--judge-model`; one per suite, so a test’s second `llm-rubric` is listed |
| `latency` with a threshold above 0, with `--target` | `latency`: the call took at most that many milliseconds |
| `cost` with a threshold above 0, with `--target` | `cost`: the call cost at most that many US dollars |

`cost` reads the cost of the model calls your function makes, as the SDK traces them. A function that makes no traced model call gives the `cost` check an error.

## What does not carry over

The converter lists each of these, with the reason, in its output and at the top of every suite file:

-   **Providers.** They are never called; the suite calls your `--target` function.
-   **Custom code:** `javascript`, `python`, `ruby` and `webhook` assertions. Rewrite them as Python checks, as in step 6.
-   **Model-graded assertions other than `llm-rubric`**, such as `factuality`, `g-eval`, `answer-relevance` and the `context-` and `model-graded-` types, and `classifier`, `moderation` and `pi`.
-   **Similarity scores:** `similar`, `levenshtein`, `rouge-`, `bleu`, `gleu`, `meteor` and `perplexity`.
-   **Checks no suite check decides the same way:** `contains-json`; `is-json` with other schemas; `equals` with a JSON value; `is-refusal` and `not-is-refusal`; red team graders; tool-call and trajectory assertions; assertions on the provider’s trace or metadata; HTML, SQL and XML formats; `word-count`; `assert-set`, `select-best`, `max-score` and `human`. Where a check comes close, the list names it so you can add it by hand.
-   **Options that change a verdict:** `transform`, `contextTransform`, a `threshold` other than on `latency` and `cost`, `rubricPrompt`, `normalizeUnicode` and `config`, and values loaded with `file://` or using template logic beyond `{{ name }}`. The assertion is not converted. `weight`, `metric` and a grading `provider` do not change the verdict, so the assertion converts and the option is listed.
-   **Test settings:** a test’s `threshold`, `metadata`, `options`, `provider`, `providers`, `prompts` and `assertScoringFunction` are listed and not applied. A test whose var is a list or a `file://` reference is not converted.
-   **Config sections** such as `scenarios`, `redteam` and `evaluateOptions`.

From results files, only the config’s `description` is kept; the rest of the config section is not copied.

## Failures and limits

-   **`No such command 'import'` or `No such command 'convert'`:** the installed SDK is older than 0.1.4. See the note at the top of this page.
-   **`Importing promptfoo results needs martian-sdk[evals]`:** install the `evals` extra, as in step 1.
-   **Exit code `2` with `Import failed:`:** the file is not promptfoo’s JSON results of the current version, has no results, gives one provider the same case twice, or gives two providers one label. Nothing was imported.
-   **Exit code `2` with `Conversion failed:`:** the config cannot be read, the `--target` file does not exist, or the output folder already holds a file the converter would write. Choose a new `--output` folder.
-   **`Nothing written: no test converts.`:** none of the tests has an assertion that converts. Exit code `2`.
-   **Case-insensitive checks** compare with Python’s case folding, where promptfoo lowercases, so a few non-English letters can compare differently.

## Next

-   [Run evals locally with a suite file](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/sdk/local-evals.md): judges, result files and running the suite in CI.
-   [Move from MLflow](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/migrate/mlflow.md) and [Move from Inspect AI](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/migrate/inspect.md) bring other tools’ results into the same data folder.

# Move a promptfoo red team

> Convert a promptfoo red team config into a run file, import its results into martian ui, and see what does not carry over. Needs SDK 0.2.0 or later.

Source: [Web version](https://docs.martiansecurity.ai/migrate/promptfoo-redteam/)

Python SDK · Any developer with a promptfoo red team config or results; no Martian account; a model key to run the converted file

Two commands move a promptfoo red team project. `martian redteam convert promptfoo` turns the `redteam` section of your config into a red team run file, and lists everything it leaves out with the reason. `martian redteam import promptfoo` brings the results you already have into `martian ui`. Neither runs promptfoo or calls its service, and promptfoo need not be installed.

Needs SDK 0.2.0 or later

Both commands are in **martian-sdk 0.2.0**. Earlier releases answer `No such command 'convert'` and `No such command 'import'` under `martian redteam`. For promptfoo eval configs and results, see [Move from promptfoo](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/migrate/promptfoo.md).

## Before you start

-   [Install the SDK](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/sdk/redteam-local.md#1-install-the-sdk) and keep its virtual environment active when you switch to your promptfoo project folder.
-   Have your `promptfooconfig.yaml` with a `redteam` section, and to import results, the JSON file `promptfoo redteam run -o results.json` writes.
-   You need no Martian account. Running the converted file needs your own model key.

## How the concepts map

| promptfoo | Martian |
| --- | --- |
| The `redteam` section of `promptfooconfig.yaml` | A version 2 run file, `redteam.yaml` |
| `targets`: an HTTP provider | `target.url`, `body`, `headers`, `response_path` |
| A Python provider | `target.file` and `function`, given with `--target`: a function that takes the message |
| `redteam.purpose` | `target.purpose` |
| `redteam.provider` | `models.attacker` and `models.judge` |
| A plugin, such as `pii:direct` | A vulnerability and its types, such as `PIILeakage` `direct_disclosure` |
| The `policy` plugin | A custom vulnerability with `criteria` |
| A strategy, such as `base64` or `crescendo` | An attack method, such as `Base64` or `Escalation` |
| The plugin’s grader, a model reading the reply | A `judge` check: suspected, evidence level 1. Text, canary, tool-call and receipt checks stated in advance confirm |
| Pass rate and exit code 100 | A gate by evidence level and severity; exit codes 0, 1 and 2 |
| The `retry` strategy | `martian redteam pin add` and `pin run` |
| Remote generation and the email | None: the run calls only your model and your agent |

## 1\. Convert the config

```sh
martian redteam convert promptfoo promptfooconfig.yaml --output converted
martian redteam validate converted/redteam.yaml
```

The first command prints what converted and a list under **Not converted**, each item with its reason, and writes the same list as comments at the top of `converted/redteam.yaml`. For the SDK’s sample config, [`examples/promptfoo-redteam/promptfooconfig.yaml`](https://github.com/MartianSecurity/martian-redteam/blob/v0.2.0/examples/promptfoo-redteam/promptfooconfig.yaml), it prints:

```text
Converted: 5 vulnerabilities, 2 attack methods, a url target, the attacker and judge model
Not converted (4):
  plugin bola: object-level authorization has no vulnerability in the catalogue
  strategy basic: promptfoo's plain plugin tests; every attack method here writes its own attack, so it needs none
  strategy jailbreak:composite: an adaptive method that promptfoo runs on its own service, or one with no attack method here (docs/redteam-methods.md)
  redteam.language: attacks are written in the attacker's language
Wrote converted/redteam.yaml. Check it with: martian redteam validate converted/redteam.yaml
```

and `validate` answers `OK: version 2, 5 vulnerabilities, 2 attacks, http target`. What converts:

-   An `http` or `https` target with a JSON body: `{{prompt}}` becomes `{{input}}`, `{{env.NAME}}` in a header becomes `${NAME}`, and a `transformResponse` that reads a path of `json`, such as `json.reply`, becomes `response_path`.
-   `purpose`; an `openai:chat:MODEL` provider as `openai:/MODEL`; `numTests` and `maxConcurrency` as the budget.
-   27 plugins onto 12 of the catalogue’s vulnerabilities, and policies. The strategies `base64`, `rot13`, `leetspeak`, `hex`, `homoglyph`, `morse`, `prompt-injection` and `citation`, and `jailbreak:tree`, `crescendo` and `best-of-n` as the attack methods `TreeSearch`, `Escalation` and `Mutation`. The same name is the same idea, not the same prompts.

What does not: plugins the converter does not map, such as `bola` (its reason says the catalogue has no such vulnerability; `martian redteam catalog` in 0.2.0 does list `BOLA`, but the converter does not map onto it), dataset plugins, `intent`, promptfoo’s service-run strategies (`jailbreak:meta`, `jailbreak:composite`, `goat`, `jailbreak:hydra` and the rest), other transforms, request and response code, session parsers, and auth settings.

A config without a `purpose` stops with exit `2` and asks for `--purpose`. A config whose strategies none convert, including promptfoo’s default (`basic`, `jailbreak:meta` and `jailbreak:composite`), stops with exit `2` and asks for `--attack`:

```sh
martian redteam convert promptfoo promptfooconfig.yaml --target agent.py:reply \
  --attack PromptInjection --output local
martian redteam run local/redteam.yaml
```

`--target` replaces the config’s target with a Python function that takes the message and returns the reply. The converted file names the config’s `redteam.provider` as its attacker and judge, so `run` needs that model’s key, set as in [Run a red team on your machine](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/sdk/redteam-local.md#2-point-it-at-your-model).

## 2\. Import the results

```sh
martian redteam import promptfoo results.json
martian ui
```

For each provider in the file, the import prints one line, such as this for the SDK’s sample [`results.json`](https://github.com/MartianSecurity/martian-redteam/blob/v0.2.0/examples/promptfoo-redteam/results.json):

```text
results.json: provider help-desk, run promptfoo-eval-rt7-2026-11-14T10-00-00-help-desk: 7 attempts, 1 vulnerable, 5 held, 1 errors; 1 suspected findings
Open them in the local UI: martian ui
```

Each provider becomes one run under **Red Team → Runs** in `martian ui`. In SDK 0.4.0 and later, importing an unchanged scan again reuses the run and preserves its reviews. Changes to recorded scan data create a separate snapshot. The report lists imported hits as **suspected** and explains its evidence limits under **Limitations of this run**.

![An imported promptfoo run with 1 suspected finding, 7 attempts and 1 error, and its limitation.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/media/screenshots/promptfoo-redteam-import.png)

A promptfoo results file imported as a red team run: every hit is suspected, and the limitation says the verdicts are promptfoo's graders.

The run keeps digests of the attacks and replies unless you set `MARTIAN_REPORT_INCLUDE_CONTENT=1`. A file of eval results is refused with exit `2` and names `martian evals import promptfoo`.

## Group saved scans by target

Use SDK 0.4.0 or later to group Promptfoo or Marsfoo scans of the same target in the local Findings inventory. Choose a stable target key when first importing those archives.

```sh
martian redteam import promptfoo baseline.json follow-up.json \
  --provider 'Library help desk' --target-key library-help-desk
```

For archives with multiple providers, give the exact displayed provider name, including any numbered suffix. The selected scans need recorded start times. Use different keys for separate targets such as staging and production. An existing run keeps its original key on reimport. To link previously unkeyed archives, import them into a separate data folder and keep the original runs and reviews.

Open [Findings](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/sdk/local-findings.md) to review recurring observations and [Remediation Reports](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/sdk/local-remediation.md) to compare saved scans. A newer linked archive can show another observation. If native attempt fingerprints are missing, an absent finding remains inconclusive.

# Find your way around the console

> Locate every customer console area, its guide and the boundary between available workflows, templates and previews.

Source: [Web version](https://docs.martiansecurity.ai/reference/console-navigation/)

The console sidebar groups current work, adversary material, history and organization access. Available controls depend on your role, project and workspace setup.

| Console area | What to do there | Guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Overview | Inspect the displayed agent page’s latest standing, declared reach and recorded coverage; a held result is not a general security guarantee | [Evidence and coverage](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/assessments/evidence-and-results.md) |
| New assessment | Configure one approved, bounded security test | [First assessment](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/get-started/first-assessment.md) and [wizard options](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/assessments/configure.md) |
| Evals | Work with datasets, runs, traces, summaries, judges and reviews | [First evaluation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/evals/first-run.md) and [Evals dashboard](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/evals/overview.md) |
| Agents | Register, validate, approve and manage authorized connections | [Connections](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/agents/connections.md) |
| Discovery | Collect inventory; inspect runtime/network evidence and explicitly enrolled call controls | [Sources](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/discovery/inventory.md), [runtime](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/discovery/runtime-and-blast-radius.md), [network observation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/discovery/network-observation.md) and [call gates](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/discovery/call-gates.md) |
| Replay | Read retained assessment evidence without executing it again | [History and exports](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/assessments/history-and-exports.md) |
| Environments | Prepare synthetic systems and manage their sandbox lifecycle | [Environments](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/environments/create-and-launch.md) |
| Pipeline | Preview and download a policy template; automated pipeline runs and waiver management are not connected to the console | [Supported SDK/CI workflow](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/sdk/ci.md) |
| Attack Library | Inspect catalogue availability, taxonomy and declared gaps, then choose supported tests | [Library coverage](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/library/coverage.md) |
| Threat Intel | Inspect the feed state; the recorded interface has no live feed connected | [Library and feed limits](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/library/coverage.md) |
| Assessments / Findings / Reports | Find saved runs, inspect observations and download the appropriate retained evidence | [Reports and exports](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/assessments/history-and-exports.md) |
| Team | Invite teammates and inspect organization roles | [Team and roles](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/workspace/team-and-roles.md) |

## Inside Evals

-   **Overview** summarizes matching native traces; it is separate from a run’s Overview and from **Monitoring**.
-   **Traces** opens native evidence, conversations, saved views and [human annotations](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/evals/trace-annotations.md).
-   **Runs** holds canonical evaluation results and the organization-wide CI sessions area; **Compare** pairs saved runs.
-   **Datasets** holds published versions and drafts. **Judges** manages saved-output criteria. **Reviews** holds assigned questions; **Quality issues** groups recorded error/failed-Boolean signals.
-   **Scoring suites** and **Monitoring** provide versioned criteria and gate history. [Choose a named project](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/evals/projects.md) deliberately; project selection changes the accessible scope.

## Account menu

The account control at the bottom of the sidebar opens **Profile**, **Theme** and **Sign out**. Profile shows your signed-in identity, role, organization and reported Agents-runtime provisioning status. It is not an account-editing or credential-issuance form. A provisioning label alone does not prove all target, model or sandbox services are ready.

**Master admin** appears only for platform operators. Organization creation/global catalogue administration and infrastructure installation remain separate from these customer tasks; ask the relevant operator when those prerequisites are absent.

Continue with [roles](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/reference/permissions.md), [supported targets](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/reference/supported-targets.md) or [troubleshooting](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/reference/troubleshooting.md).

# Glossary

> Plain definitions for the words used in Martian customer workflows.

Source: [Web version](https://docs.martiansecurity.ai/reference/glossary/)

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Agent | The application or callback being tested, with its own intended rules and tools |
| Assessment | A bounded security test against an authorized agent |
| Attack technique | A supported way to try to cause an unwanted outcome |
| Assurance pack | A published scenario-backed option with specific compatibility and outcome-check requirements |
| Baseline | The chosen reference run or observed starting state; its meaning depends on the workflow |
| Call gate | Customer SDK enforcement at entry to an explicitly enrolled named model/tool call |
| Connection | Approved interface/address/credential contract for reaching an agent |
| Dataset | A collection of inputs and expected answers |
| Dataset version | An immutable published dataset snapshot |
| Endpoint-only | Assessment scope limited to the agent’s exposed interface |
| Environment | A saved configuration of isolated synthetic business systems |
| Evals | Dataset-based response evaluation and related saved-output analysis |
| Exact match | Equality after stripping surrounding whitespace and ignoring case |
| Finding | A recorded observed problem with its evidence and verification limits |
| Judge | A configured scorer that returns typed feedback, sometimes using a model |
| Outcome check | A supported independent observation of the relevant business state |
| Oracle | A trusted check of the claimed outcome, independent of the attacking model’s opinion |
| Carrier / implant | The message, document or tool descriptor carrying an untrusted attack payload, and the payload inserted into it |
| No-implant control | A comparable test without that inserted payload, used to check whether the effect depends on the attack |
| World epoch | An identifier for a particular initialized or restored sandbox state; different epochs can represent different test worlds |
| Project | An organization-scoped Evals grouping for runs and related work |
| Provenance | Recorded identities, versions, authorizations and revisions explaining where results came from |
| Replay | Inspection of retained execution evidence; it does not itself mean a new live execution |
| Reproduction | A distinct repeat of a test under the recorded verification conditions |
| Review queue | Selected saved results and their required human questions |
| Sandbox | An isolated running copy of a supported synthetic business application |
| Scorer | A defined calculation or judgment applied to a result |
| Seed data | Synthetic records used to initialize a sandbox world |
| Session | A grouping of recorded conversation turns when that identity was captured |
| Suite | An immutable versioned set of scoring criteria and quality thresholds |
| Trace | A retained execution/message record and its associated attributes/evidence |
| Viewer / member / admin / owner | Customer roles with different allowed actions |

[Choose a workflow](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/get-started/concepts.md) or [check permissions](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/reference/permissions.md).

---

# Budgets, limits and evidence

> Understand bounded execution, stopping, provenance and evidence coverage.

Source: [Web version](https://docs.martiansecurity.ai/reference/limits/)

Use the live launch form and readiness messages for the active environment’s policy. These are ceilings and evidence boundaries, not security guarantees.

## Assessments

The chosen depth controls admitted work. The examined Light profile defaults to ceilings of **30 target calls**, **100 model calls** and **360 seconds**; organization/server policy can reduce or reject that request. The interface, target authorization and compatible execution mode can further limit concurrency, supported checks and reproduction.

Cancellation requests a stop. It does not undo a request already sent or prove a provider has physically finished. Inspect final state, skipped/failed checks and retained evidence.

## Evals

| Area | Current boundary |
| --- | --- |
| Target-call budget | API 1–1,000 selected records; UI choices 100 / 250 / 500 / 1,000 |
| Small tutorial | Use a three-record dataset: budget 100 is an upper bound, not 100 mandatory requests |
| Concurrent target runs | One queued/running evaluation per organization, across projects |
| Concurrent scoring jobs | One active scoring job per organization, separate from target admission |
| Target execution | Sequential; ACTIVE usable records within the selected budget |
| Human queue | 1–100 selected results, 1–8 unique required questions |
| Bulk dataset/review actions | Up to 100 selected records per action |
| Trace query page | Up to 100 rows; default 25 |
| Bounded trace exports/scans | Limits apply at 1,000 matches; narrow filters when a complete export is refused |
| Dataset import | Up to 20 MiB and 100,000 records; the whole invalid upload is rejected |

**Stop after current request** retains an in-flight result, prevents the next target call and marks remaining selected records skipped. Scoring stop similarly retains the in-flight judgment. Reopening, exporting or reviewing saved values does not execute the target again.

## Scores

Canonical exact match compares stripped, case-folded actual and expected strings. Punctuation and extra text still matter. Other scores preserve their own definition and type. Numeric/category/text feedback must not be presented as a Boolean pass rate. Missing token or cost data is unknown, not zero.

## Provenance and coverage

Published dataset versions and runs retain pinned identities/digests. A declared agent artifact revision is useful provenance; an agent’s name cannot establish its model or prompt version. Historical data and bounded runtime observations do not independently verify effective access, predict an incident or prove a loss ceiling.

A clean reproduction, negative control, independent business check and model opinion establish different things. Read [assessment evidence](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/assessments/reproduction-and-limits.md) and [Discovery evidence](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/discovery/runtime-and-blast-radius.md) before interpreting them.

---

# Roles and permissions

> Check the minimum role for each customer task.

Source: [Web version](https://docs.martiansecurity.ai/reference/permissions/)

Permissions apply within your organization. Your console session and a machine API key are separate forms of access. This table summarizes the current source contract; the live interface can additionally withhold an action when setup, target approval or environment policy is not ready.

| Task | Viewer | Member | Admin / owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Browse authorized assessments, results, datasets and Evals history | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Launch/stop assessments and Evals | No | Yes | Yes |
| Create/configure environments and manage their sandbox lifecycle | No | Yes | Yes |
| Register, validate, approve, rotate or disable agent connections | No | No | Yes |
| Import/edit dataset drafts | No | Yes | Yes |
| Publish an organization dataset | No | No | Yes |
| Create/archive Evals projects; register custom model judges | No | No | Yes |
| Score saved outputs, create suites/questions, complete assigned reviews | No | Yes | Yes |
| Triage quality issues | No | Yes | Yes |
| Assign another eligible reviewer; manage organization API keys and team invitations | No | No | Yes |

Platform-admin organization and global-dataset administration are separate operator capabilities. These customer guides do not grant them.

## Machine credentials

A scoped API key authorizes only its granted capabilities and resource restrictions. It does not sign a person in to the console, enable a hosted feature or provide a target model’s credentials. Existing Evals keys do not automatically gain hosted redteam rights.

[Create and configure an SDK key](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/sdk/install-and-configure.md) and [read team management](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/workspace/team-and-roles.md) for the actual controls.

## If a control is missing or disabled

1.  Confirm the organization and your current role.
2.  Read the page’s setup/readiness message.
3.  Check target approval and the selected project’s state.
4.  Ask an admin for the specific missing role or capability. Do not share an owner’s password or API token.

# Supported agent targets

> Choose an interface supported by the workflow you intend to run.

Source: [Web version](https://docs.martiansecurity.ai/reference/supported-targets/)

An approved connection defines how Martian reaches your agent. Registering a URL does not establish every workflow is compatible with it.

| Interface | Assessments | Dataset Evals | Main prerequisite |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Stateless HTTP chat | Supported | Supported | Validated, approved and active connection with chat authorization |
| Streamable HTTP MCP | Supported | Unsupported | Selected entry tool and approved argument/response contract |
| Public HTTPS browser chat | Supported, endpoint-only and serial | Unsupported | Compatible chat interface; public HTTPS on port 443 |
| Session-backed HTTP | Supported where the approved session contract applies | Unsupported | Approved session create/use/cleanup contract |
| Customer local callback through SDK | SDK redteam workflow | SDK prediction function | Correct SDK connection/scopes; target/provider credentials remain in your process |

## HTTP and MCP access

Normal customer endpoints require public HTTPS. Internal demo host allowlists and local-HTTP development settings are operator-owned exceptions; they are not a way to register an arbitrary private address from the customer console.

MCP validation discovers tools and binds approval to the selected schema. Revalidate after the contract, credentials or sandbox bindings change. A changed dynamic connection does not silently fall back to a legacy target.

## Browser chat

The browser executor supports the approved website flow and optional username/password website sign-in. URL validation checks URL/access configuration, not successful login. SSO, MFA, CAPTCHA, handoff and unsupported chat discovery can stop execution. Website sign-in is distinct from an attested synthetic business identity.

The chat interface must support starting a fresh conversation after setup. Use an in-place conversation reset so the browser can stay on the approved page. If the reset times out, inspect the [saved action and recovery notice](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/assessments/evidence-and-results.md#read-a-browser-run-that-needs-attention).

## Evals and saved outputs

A dataset run sends selected active inputs to its approved HTTP target. Saved-output scoring, reviews and comparisons use retained values; they do not resend the target request. Paid model judging requires its own readiness and acknowledgement.

**Next:** [Set up a connection](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/agents/connections.md) or [use SDK callbacks](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/sdk/redteam.md).

---

# Troubleshooting

> Resolve common access, connection, run, dataset and scoring failures safely.

Source: [Web version](https://docs.martiansecurity.ai/reference/troubleshooting/)

Start with the action’s recorded state and exact error. Refresh retained history before submitting duplicate work.

| Symptom | Check | Safe next action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Invitation is incomplete, expired or revoked | Correct recipient, organization address, latest link | Ask the inviter to replace it; keep links private |
| Sign-in works but a control is missing | Role and selected organization | Use the permissions table; ask for the specific required authority |
| Agent exists but cannot run | Draft/validation/approval/connection changes | Complete validation and approval; rotate/reapprove changed credentials |
| Browser URL validates but assessment fails | Website login, SSO/MFA/CAPTCHA/chat discovery | Inspect the run error; URL validation was not login success |
| Evals says setup is pending or needs review | Organization readiness, selected project | Use Refresh setup; ask an admin to resolve a failed/uncertain setup |
| A run is refused as busy | Organization-wide target/scoring admission | Wait for the active work; inspect its stop/final state |
| Launch response was lost | Existing saved run and launch request | Inspect/recover saved work before creating another request |
| Needs attention retains a submission error after refresh | Original run ID and runtime admission | Ask your operator to inspect that same campaign; a successful refresh response or an ended label does not prove downstream execution stopped |
| Dataset import is rejected | Preview row errors, fields, duplicate IDs, file format | Correct the entire upload; invalid input is not partially merged |
| Draft changed during publish | Current revision and validation hash | Refresh and review; publish the intended new revision |
| Published global dataset is read-only | Reserved martian: catalogue entry | Use Copy to my datasets, then edit your organization’s copy |
| Exact match is false unexpectedly | Complete actual/expected text | Check punctuation, extra prose and formatting; stripped case differences alone are ignored |
| Model judging unavailable | Model access, organization readiness, acknowledgement | Use supported code scoring or ask the admin; never invent missing feedback |
| Review saved but queue still pending | All required questions and native feedback verification | Wait/refresh; verify each latest required answer, not only the last clicked row |
| Export refuses too many results | Match count and active filters | Narrow the query; do not treat a partial page as the whole dataset |
| SDK exits with a setup error | Exact installed version, variables, scopes and supported command | Follow SDK configuration |

## Keep evidence useful

Record the run ID, approximate time, action, visible error and the steps already tried. Exclude passwords, tokens, cookies, customer prompts and private exports from shared issues. Use synthetic examples when reproducing a problem.

## Stop and uncertainty

A stop acknowledgement is not proof that an in-flight provider call has completed. Wait for final state and inspect retained work. Do not repeatedly retry an uncertain paid operation just to obtain a passing result.

**Next:** [Permissions](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/reference/permissions.md), [limits](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/reference/limits.md) or the [SDK configuration guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/sdk/install-and-configure.md).

---

# Use these docs with an AI assistant

> Copy a complete page or share a public Markdown link that an assistant can read without signing in.

Source: [Web version](https://docs.martiansecurity.ai/reference/using-with-agents/)

Every documentation page has **Copy page** above its title. It copies the article as Markdown, including code examples, prerequisites, verification notices and screenshot links.

## Share a page

1.  Open the guide you need.
2.  Select **Copy page** and paste it into your assistant’s chat.
3.  To share a link instead, open the arrow beside **Copy page** and select **Copy agent link**. Paste the link into your chat and ask the assistant to read it.

The agent link opens a public, plain-text Markdown copy on GitHub. It needs no account, JavaScript or product access. This is an independent HTTPS access path alongside the documentation website. The content includes a link back to the web version.

**View Markdown** opens the same plain-text page. Use it if your browser blocks clipboard access, or if JavaScript is disabled. Select and copy its text manually.

## Give an assistant more context

-   [Agent index](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/llms.txt): a list of pages with short descriptions and direct Markdown links. The page menu also links to this index.
-   [Complete documentation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/llms-full.txt): every page in one text file. It is larger; start with a specific guide when possible.

The site publishes the same files at `/markdown/<page-path>.md`, `/llms.txt` and `/llms-full.txt`. Each HTML page advertises its Markdown alternatives in its document head, so tools that inspect page metadata can discover them.

## Keep the guide’s limits in context

A copied guide includes its role requirements, compatibility details and product limits. Include your installed SDK version or workspace edition when asking for help with a guide.

These are public instructions. Sharing a page does not give an assistant access to your workspace, API keys or authenticated product. Supply only the context you intend to share.

# Scan in the console

> Upload a folder, read the result by category, finding and evidence, and triage, approve and monitor what you scanned.

Source: [Web version](https://docs.martiansecurity.ai/scanner/console/)

Current beta console · owner, admin or member (start); any member (read); owner or admin (triage, approve, delete stored files)

Scan a skill, an MCP configuration, a plugin or a repository from the console and read what the Scanner found.

## Before you start

-   Your organization has the Scanner turned on ([who has it](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/scanner/overview.md#who-has-it)). Without it the **Scanner** group is not in the sidebar.
-   You are an owner, admin or member to start a scan; any member reads scans.
-   Have the folder ready, or a ZIP of it of at most 50 MiB (your organization’s limit may be lower).

## Start a scan

1.  In the sidebar, open **Scanner → New scan**.
2.  Under **Type**, choose what you are scanning: a skill, an MCP server, a plugin, a sub-agent, harness configuration, agent code or a repository.
3.  Under **Name**, give it a name. Scans of the same type and name belong to one add-on, so later scans are compared with earlier ones.
4.  Drop the folder or the ZIP file on the page, or choose it.
5.  Select **Start scan**. The result page follows the scan stage by stage.

A refused upload says why and names the limit it broke: the archive’s size, its number of files, or the organization’s scans for the day.

## Read the result

-   **Categories** shows each category as flagged, clear or not checked, with the stages a not-checked one is missing.
-   **Findings** lists each finding with its severity, evidence level, file and line. Select one to open the file with the cited lines marked.
-   **References** lists every link, package and repository the files point at, with what the registry answered, when, and when it is checked again.
-   **Coverage** lists the files that were skipped or not inspected and why.
-   **Download JSON** and **Download SARIF** export the scan.

## Triage, approve and monitor

1.  **Findings** across scans: an owner or admin accepts a finding (with a reason and an end date), waives it, or reopens it. Each action is in the audit log.
2.  **Policy** sets the severity of a rule for your organization, and the notifications for new findings, drift and voided approvals.
3.  **Add-ons** shows each add-on’s latest scan. An owner or admin **approves** the content digest of a completed scan. When the add-on’s content or what it points at changes, the approval is void and the add-on shows **changed since approval**.
4.  Add-ons from a registry are fetched again weekly, and what they point at is re-checked daily.

## Delete the stored files

The uploaded archive is kept for your organization’s retention period after its newest scan ([limits and data](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/scanner/limits-and-data.md#how-long-uploaded-files-are-kept)). An owner or admin can delete it sooner: open the scan, and under **This scan** select **Delete the stored files**. The scan and its findings stay.

## Next

-   [Limits, usage and data](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/scanner/limits-and-data.md)
-   [Pull requests through GitHub (coming soon)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/scanner/github-app.md)

# Limits, usage and data

> The Scanner's limits, where owners and admins read their organization's usage, and what is stored of scanned content and for how long.

Source: [Web version](https://docs.martiansecurity.ai/scanner/limits-and-data/)

Current beta console · owner or admin (usage, retention, deletion); any member (limits)

## Limits

The master admin sets your organization’s Scanner limits when they turn the Scanner on:

| Limit | Default | When it is reached |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scans a day | 200 | A new scan is refused (`429`) with the limit named |
| Largest upload | 50 MiB | The upload is refused (`413`) with the limit |
| Files in one upload | 5,000 entries, 10 MiB per file, 200 MiB unpacked | The upload is refused with the limit |
| Model analysis requests in one scan | 24 | The scan’s later passes are listed as not run |

An organization may also start at most 30 scans a minute.

## Usage

Owners and admins see what the organization’s scanning used over the last 30 days under **Scanner → Settings → Usage**: scans by state, scans today against the daily limit, files read, references resolved and not attempted, model calls and tokens, minutes of add-ons run in a sandbox, and the bundles stored. Every figure is counted from the scans themselves.

## How long uploaded files are kept

| What is stored | How long |
| --- | --- |
| The uploaded or fetched archive (the bundle) | Your organization’s retention after its newest scan: 30 days unless an owner or admin changes it under **Scanner → Settings → Uploaded files** (1 to 3,650 days) |
| Each scan’s record: the file list with each file’s hash, the coverage, the references and what the registries answered | While the organization exists |
| Findings, each with an excerpt of at most 1,000 characters of the line a rule matched | While the organization exists. They are what gates, approvals and triage were decided on |
| Pages, files and repositories the Scanner fetched | Not stored. They are hashed, and the scan’s working folder is removed when it ends |

-   When a bundle’s retention ends it is deleted from storage; the scan and its findings stay. The same files can be scanned again by uploading them again.
-   An owner or admin deletes a scan’s stored files at once from the scan’s page (**Delete the stored files**). Every scan of the same files shares them. The deletion is in the audit log.
-   A legal hold on the organization stops every deletion while it holds.
-   Deleting the organization deletes its stored files and its Scanner records. Its audit log is kept.

## Next

-   [What the Scanner checks](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/scanner/overview.md)
-   [Self-hosted](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/scanner/self-hosted.md)

# Method and measured results

> How the Scanner finds direct and indirect issues, what each evidence level means, what it does not claim, and its measured precision and recall on its labelled corpus.

Source: [Web version](https://docs.martiansecurity.ai/scanner/method/)

Current beta console · Anyone evaluating or using the Scanner

This page says how the Skills / MCP / Plugin Scanner reaches each finding, what a finding at each evidence level may and may not mean, and how accurate it is on the corpus it is measured on. Every number here comes from the Scanner’s accuracy report for the release this page describes. A number from another corpus, or from a scan with fewer stages, can be very different.

## Direct issues: what the files themselves say

The Scanner reads every file of an add-on, not only `SKILL.md`: scripts, reference documents, MCP server configurations, plugin and marketplace manifests, hooks, settings, sub-agents, rules files, lockfiles and the agent’s own source code. Nothing it reads is run. Each file is parsed into the facts a client would act on (the commands a hook runs, the servers an MCP configuration starts, the tools a skill pre-approves, the agent a framework builds), each citing a file and a line.

Rules then look for what is wrong in the text and in those facts:

-   **Pattern rules** match text: a download piped to a shell, a read of `~/.aws/credentials`, an instruction that tells the agent to hide something. The rules for hidden instructions match the text as a model reads it, with invisible characters removed and look-alike letters folded.
-   **Structural rules** test the parsed facts: a hook that runs a command when a session starts, a setting that turns off approval, an MCP server that is not pinned.
-   **Code rules** read agent source without running it: a tool whose input reaches a shell, model output that reaches execution, an agent that can delegate to an ungated action.

Zip and tar archives inside the add-on are opened, one level deep, and their members read the same way. A file the Scanner could not read (too large, binary, an archive it does not open) is listed in the scan’s coverage, never treated as clean.

## Indirect issues: what the files point at

A `SKILL.md` can be clean and still tell the agent to read and follow a page, or run a package, that is not safe. The Scanner follows the chain in seven steps, and each step states what it found and where it stopped:

1.  **Extract every reference, with its role.** Every link, repository, package, domain, container image, cloud host, local path and command the files name, and what the agent is told to do with it: follow it (instruction source), run it (executed code), install it (dependency), read it (data), or nothing (link).
2.  **Ask who is behind it.** GitHub, the package registries, the domain registries, DNS and the MCP Registry are asked about each reference, and every answer is kept as a receipt: what was asked, from where, when, and what came back. A repository whose owner was deleted, a package name nobody has published or a domain anyone can register is reported as a name that can be claimed. The Scanner never claims it.
3.  **Fetch what it points at, safely.** Only public addresses, every redirect checked again, with caps on size and time. A fetch cut at a cap is partial, never complete.
4.  **Judge the content against the add-on’s stated purpose.** A model is asked whether the fetched content asks the agent for something outside what the add-on says it is for: reading credentials, sending data out, switching off approval, hiding from the user, fetching and running more code. Every answer must quote the passage it relies on, the quotation is checked again, and more than half of the passes must agree. The model may add a finding. It can never clear or lower one.
5.  **Check whether the Scanner was shown something else.** Each instruction source is fetched as the Scanner and as an agent-like client, and a difference is reported.
6.  **Record a hash and check again.** What was fetched is hashed, and a change since the last scan is reported. References are checked again on their own schedule between scans.
7.  **Say what could not be checked.** A reference ends as resolved, does not exist, unresolved (with the reason) or not attempted. Unresolved and not attempted are never clean.

An organization can turn off sending content to a model. Its scans then stop at level 3, and say so.

## Evidence levels

Each finding carries the highest level its evidence reached:

| Level | What was observed | The finding may say | It must not say |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0\. Inventory | The add-on was parsed | It references X, runs Y, is pinned or not | Anything about risk |
| 1\. Pattern | Text or code matches a rule | A pattern linked to this behavior is here | “Malicious”, or that the behavior happens |
| 2\. Structural | A deterministic check of the parsed facts | This is so, with the values shown | Intent |
| 3\. Resolved | A reference was checked at a stated time from a stated place | At that time it did not exist, redirected, or was registered on this date | That it has been or will be exploited |
| 4\. Assessed | Linked content was fetched, hashed and judged against the stated purpose | This content asks for Z, outside the stated purpose | That an agent will comply |
| 5\. Observed | The add-on ran in a sandbox with decoy credentials | In N of M runs it did this | That a clean run means safe |
| 6\. Corroborated | A lower level plus an independent match or a human review | “Malicious” or “compromised” |  |

## What a result means, and what it does not claim

A clean result means: no findings at the levels the scan reached, with the coverage it states, at the time it ran. It is not a verdict that the add-on is safe.

-   **A category is clear only when every stage it needs ran.** Otherwise it is not checked, and the result says which stage did not run.
-   **A sandbox run proves presence, never absence.** An add-on that did nothing in a run may act later or elsewhere.
-   **Every cap is a way to hide.** A file over the size limit, an archive the Scanner does not open, a fetch cut at its cap: each is listed, and the categories that depend on it are not reported clear.
-   **A claimable name can be wrong.** GitHub does not say whether a freed name is retired, so “this owner name can be claimed” can be wrong for a once-popular repository.
-   **The model can miss.** Published defenses against prompt injection aimed at a model judge have been broken under adaptive attack. That is why the model can only add findings and why its findings stand on a quoted passage.
-   **The Scanner reads files, not accounts or machines.** Connectors and skills held in a vendor’s account, and what is installed on a developer’s laptop, are not seen.

## How accuracy is measured

The Scanner is scored on a labelled corpus kept with its source. Each sample is a folder scanned as one unit and labelled with the categories a correct scan reports for it. A category whose ground truth is not settled for a sample is marked uncertain and not scored.

| Samples | Benign | Harmful | What they are |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 40 | 40 | 0 | Martian’s own skills, including eight that describe attack techniques in plain words, as hard negatives |
| 9 | 5 | 4 | Martian’s demonstration MCP server and agent: its defensive prompts, and deliberately weak twins of them |
| 4 | 4 | 0 | Public skills from Anthropic’s Apache-2.0 plugin directory |
| 36 | 16 | 20 | Synthetic samples written for the corpus: harmful ones for each content category, and benign twins of them |
| 9 | 1 | 8 | Indirect-case fixtures: clean add-ons that point at a deleted repository owner, a renamed owner, an unpublished package, a look-alike domain, a page that changes after the scan, a page that cloaks, a five-hop chain to an unpublished package, an unregistered MCP host, and one benign twin |
| 37 | 0 | 37 | Bypass fixtures: one inert sample for each published way past a skill or MCP scanner that Martian’s research records (40 classes, some sharing a sample) |
| 14 | 0 | 14 | Attack-library fixtures: one inert sample for each mechanism of the attack records on agent add-ons in Martian’s attack library |
| **149** | **66** | **83** |  |

The indirect-case fixtures are offline: each carries recorded answers from the registries and the pages it names, and the model’s analysis is replayed from recorded answers of the Scanner’s analysis model. No live network or model is used when the corpus is scored.

For each sample and category, the labels determine whether a finding counts as a true or false positive. With no finding, the category counts as a true or false negative only when the scan checked it. When a required stage did not run, the category counts as **not checked**.

## Measured results

Per category. TP, FP, FN and TN are counts of samples. “Not checked” is the number of harmful and benign samples on which the scan did not check the category: the resolve and fetch categories are checked only where there is something to resolve, and prompt injection only where the model analysis ran.

| Category | TP | FP | FN | TN | Not checked (harmful / benign) | Precision | Recall |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Supply chain | 23 | 0 | 0 | 2 | 0 / 118 | 23 of 23 | 23 of 23 |
| Distribution credibility | 1 | 0 | 0 | 2 | 0 / 144 | 1 of 1 | 1 of 1 |
| External instruction source | 4 | 0 | 0 | 3 | 3 / 138 | 4 of 4 | 4 of 4 |
| Server integrity | 1 | 0 | 0 | 5 | 1 / 142 | 1 of 1 | 1 of 1 |
| Prompt injection | 5 | 0 | 0 | 60 | 5 / 78 | 5 of 5 | 5 of 5 |
| Data exfiltration | 8 | 0 | 0 | 134 | 0 / 0 | 8 of 8 | 8 of 8 |
| Excessive actions | 5 | 0 | 1 | 141 | 0 / 0 | 5 of 5 | 5 of 6 |
| Hidden behavior | 28 | 0 | 0 | 117 | 0 / 0 | 28 of 28 | 28 of 28 |
| Unsafe configuration | 13 | 0 | 0 | 135 | 0 / 0 | 13 of 13 | 13 of 13 |
| Agent code weakness | 5 | 0 | 0 | 142 | 0 / 0 | 5 of 5 | 5 of 5 |

Per evidence level. A finding is true or false by the same labels; recall at a level counts the expected categories caught at that level or above.

| Level | True findings | False findings | Recall at or above |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0\. Inventory | 5 | 0 | 99% |
| 1\. Pattern | 44 | 0 | 96% |
| 2\. Structural | 62 | 0 | 67% |
| 3\. Resolved | 8 | 0 | 20% |
| 4\. Assessed | 23 | 0 | 16% |
| 5\. Observed | 0 | 0 | 0% |
| 6\. Corroborated | 0 | 0 | 0% |

Most harmful samples carry their problem in their own text or structure, so most are caught at levels 1 and 2; few have a reference to resolve or content to fetch, which is why recall at levels 3 and 4 is low.

No rule that runs by default reported a category on a benign sample that the sample is not labelled for.

## What these numbers are, and are not

-   **They are bound to this corpus.** Published evaluations of other scanners show the same engine scoring under 10% or over 90% recall depending on the corpus and the mode. These numbers say how the Scanner does on these samples, not on the add-ons you will scan.
-   **The counts are small.** Several categories have one to eight harmful samples. “5 of 5” is not evidence of no misses in general, and no false positive on 66 benign samples is not a false-positive rate for the field.
-   **Most samples are Martian’s.** The harmful samples were written for the corpus (the bypass and attack-library fixtures reproduce published techniques as inert samples), and most benign ones are Martian’s own skills and agents. Third-party sets of real malicious add-ons are not in it: their terms forbid redistribution or they hold working malware, so they are listed by name and not scored.
-   **The indirect case is measured on fixtures we built.** No public dataset labels a clean add-on that points at hostile or claimable content, so the nine fixtures are the only indirect-case measurement there is. They replay recorded answers; a live registry or page can answer differently.
-   **Level 4 is measured on recorded answers of one model.** A live model, or another model, can flag more or less.
-   **The resolve and fetch categories are checked only where there is something to resolve,** and prompt injection only where the model analysis ran. On the other samples they are not checked, which is why their “not checked” counts are high.
-   **Levels 5 and 6 are not measured.** The corpus has no sandbox runs and no corroborated samples.

## Known limits

What the stages that exist cannot see. Each is reported as not checked, skipped or not inspected where it applies; none is reported clear.

-   **Natural-language attacks.** Patterns catch known phrasings only. A ciphered, translated, paraphrased or payload-less instruction, or one split across tool descriptions, needs the model analysis; where it did not run, prompt injection is not checked. A data-exfiltration instruction in plain words with no path or command is not caught by a rule.
-   **Behavior at run time.** A trigger that waits for a date, an environment or a number of calls, and a payload decided at run time, are seen only by running the add-on. A trigger whose payload is in the files is caught by the payload’s rule.
-   **Remote content.** A remote MCP server is listed under one client identity; an answer that differs by identity or by number of calls is not compared.
-   **Across files.** Values are followed inside one file. A download to a fixed path run by another file is caught; other data passed between files is not followed.
-   **Opaque content.** Archives are opened one level deep, and 7-Zip, RAR, zstandard and lone gzip streams not at all; binary data, PDFs and legacy Office documents are not read. Each is listed as not inspected.

---

# What the Scanner checks

> The Skills / MCP / Plugin Scanner reads the files you give an agent and reports what is wrong with them, at a stated level of evidence and with the coverage of each scan.

Source: [Web version](https://docs.martiansecurity.ai/scanner/overview/)

Current beta console · Any member of an Enterprise organization with the Scanner

The Skills / MCP / Plugin Scanner is the third part of Martian Protect. It reads the files an agent is given (skills, MCP server configurations, plugins, sub-agents, hooks, settings, rules files and the agent’s own code) and reports what is wrong with them, including the indirect case: a clean `SKILL.md` that tells the agent to read and follow a link or a file that is not safe.

The Scanner checks the files you give an agent. It does not replace [Red Team](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/get-started/first-assessment.md), which tests what the agent does. A Scanner finding never starts a Red Team run; you start one on purpose.

## Who has it

**Invite-only beta.** Use the Scanner in the hosted Enterprise console when your workspace has Scanner access. Ask your Martian contact to enable it for your organization. [Scanner limits and data](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/scanner/limits-and-data.md).

**Upcoming.** GitHub pull-request scanning and the Scanner for [planned On-Premises deployments](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/scanner/self-hosted.md) are upcoming. See [Editions](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/get-started/editions.md).

You can try the public [single-file scan](https://www.martiansecurity.ai/scan/) without signing in. It checks the text of one `SKILL.md` or MCP configuration. It skips external lookups and model analysis, and discards the file and result.

Once it is on:

-   owners, admins and members start scans, and every member reads them;
-   owners and admins triage findings, approve add-ons and change the Scanner’s settings.

## What a scan reads

You upload a folder as a ZIP file in the console, or name a package or skill in a registry. Each scan is of one **content digest**: the SHA-256 over every file’s path and hash. The same files give the same digest, so an approval names exactly the content it approved.

The scan runs in stages. Each stage that ran is listed in the result, and each that did not is too:

| Stage | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| Unpack, inventory, parse | Reads every file, hashes it, and works out what each one is and which agent clients load it. A file it could not read is listed, never treated as clean |
| Rules | Pattern and structural rules: dangerous commands and downloads, hidden text, hooks and settings that run commands, permissions, MCP server configuration, and data flows in the agent’s own code |
| References and resolve | Every link, repository, package, domain, image and command the files point at, and what the registries say about each: a package nobody has published, a domain anyone can register, a repository whose owner was deleted, a version with a known vulnerability |
| Fetch and assess | What the add-on tells the agent to read or run, fetched and judged against what the add-on says it is for. A model may add a finding; it never clears one |

## Evidence levels

Every finding states how strong its evidence is. A clean result means no findings at the levels the scan reached, with its coverage, at that time.

| Level | Name | Means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | Inventory | The file exists and is loaded by these clients |
| 1 | Pattern | A rule matched the text |
| 2 | Structural | The parsed structure shows it (a hook that runs a command, an unpinned server) |
| 3 | Resolved | A registry or address answered (the package does not exist; the domain is unregistered) |
| 4 | Assessed | A model, citing the passage, judged it outside the add-on’s purpose, and two passes agreed |
| 5 | Observed | It was seen when the add-on ran in a sandbox |
| 6 | Corroborated | An independent source agrees. Only level 6 is called malicious |

A scan whose organization does not allow sending content to a model stops at level 3, and says so.

## Coverage

Each result shows every category as **flagged** (a finding is in it), **clear** (every stage it needs ran and nothing was found) or **not checked** (a stage it needs did not run, or did not cover everything). A reference the Scanner did not ask about is **not attempted**, never clean, and a category that depends on it is not checked.

## Next

-   [Scan in the console](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/scanner/console.md)
-   [Limits, usage and data](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MartianSecurity/martian-security-docs/main/public/markdown/scanner/limits-and-data.md)
